_readme: Rule tables for tools/format_commentary.py. Every rule has a stable id so a
correction later is a data edit, not a parser rewrite.
Sorted longest-first at load time, so 'केचित्तु' wins over 'केचित्' and
'इत्यत उक्तम्' over 'उक्तम्'. Do not rely on the order here.
introducers_exact match at the END of a word, not as standalone words:
sandhi joins them, and the corpus's own 'कोषोक्तेराह' is exactly that case.
p1_require_citation_ending: a Pattern-1 pratika's LAST word must end in one
of pratika_suffixes. Without it the rule captured 77 characters of ordinary
prose ending in 'वा' -- an introducer followed by whatever reached the next
danda. A pratika is a quoted lemma plus its citation particle, so requiring
the citation particle is the definition, not a heuristic.

_note: The spec was written in ASCII | and ||. The corpus uses U+0964 DANDA;
a double danda is TWO U+0964, and U+0965 also occurs. All forms are
accepted and none is ever rewritten into another.
_p2_note: Pattern 2 accepts danda delimiters as of 15 Sep 2026, on the project lead's
decision. It was restricted to ASCII pipes before that because section 11 of
the brief defines it as delimiter + one or two words + delimiter while section
29 forbids reading भिन्नेति ।। as a pratika -- and in danda-punctuated prose
those are the same shape, so honouring both meant declining to fire on a danda.
With it on, the precision now rests entirely on the two constraints that
remain: at most two words, and the last of them must end in a citation
particle. Those are what keep it from tagging ordinary sentence endings.
Set back to 'pipes_only' to restore the earlier behaviour.

_note: What may sit between an introducer and its pratika. The dash forms
carry P1B, which is the shape the real corpus actually uses.
A pratika is a quoted LEMMA plus its citation particle. These are the
particle with no lemma in front of it -- ordinary commentary joinery,
not a quotation of anything. P1C found इति । and इत्यर्थः । as
'pratikas' in SM6:6 and SM6:12 until this list existed.
